We treat webhooks as the source of truth, make every handler idempotent, and reconcile Stripe events against your own records so a dropped or duplicated event never silently corrupts an account. Whether you are launching a first paid tier or replacing a tangle of manual invoicing, we wire billing into the product so finance, support, and customers all see the same numbers.

points.title: Subscriptions and plan changes

faqs.answer: Every handler is idempotent and verifies the Stripe signature, so a retried or duplicated event is safe to process twice. intro: Moving to Shopify from WooCommerce, Magento, OpenCart, BigCommerce, or a custom platform is far more than a product CSV. Customer accounts and password-reset flows, historic orders, product variants, metafields, tax and shipping zones, and payment-provider switching all have to carry across correctly, and the URLs that earned your search rankings have to redirect one to one so you do not lose traffic on launch day.

We start by auditing the source platform's data model, then map every entity into Shopify using the APIs, Matrixify, and custom scripts chosen for what the old system actually exposes. The migration is rehearsed as a dry run on a development store before the live cut-over, so the switch is a checklist that has already been run through twice rather than a leap of faith.

points.title: Data mapping and audit
points.body: We document the source platform's products, variants, customers, orders, and metafields, and define exactly how each maps into Shopify before anything moves.

points.title: SEO-preserving redirects
points.body: Every old URL is redirected one to one to its Shopify equivalent so rankings, backlinks, and traffic survive the replatform.

points.title: Customers and historic orders

points.title: Tax, shipping, and payments

points.title: Rehearsed cut-over

points.title: Post-launch verification
points.body: We monitor for 404s, checkout errors, and indexing changes immediately after launch and fix regressions while the migration is fresh.

faqs.question: Will migrating to Shopify hurt our search rankings?
faqs.answer: Not if the redirects are done properly. The biggest SEO risk in any replatform is broken URLs, so we map every old URL to its Shopify equivalent with one-to-one redirects, preserve title and metadata structure where it makes sense, and monitor indexing after launch. Done this way, rankings typically hold through the move.

faqs.question: Can you migrate customer accounts and historic orders?
faqs.answer: Yes. Customers migrate with a password-reset flow because password hashes cannot transfer between platforms, and historic orders come across so support and reporting stay intact. We reconcile counts against the source store so nothing is silently dropped.

faqs.question: How do you avoid downtime during the switch?
faqs.answer: We rehearse the migration as a dry run on a Shopify development store first, then run the live cut-over from a checklist that has already been tested. DNS, redirects, and payments are sequenced so the storefront stays available, and we verify checkout end to end before announcing the new store.

title: Sanity CMS development

headline: we build Sanity into a content platform your editors trust and your front end can query with GROQ.

points.title: Structured content modelling

points.title: Custom Studio configuration

points.title: GROQ-powered delivery

points.title: Live preview and drafts

points.title: Portable, multi-channel content

faqs.question: When is Sanity a better choice than WordPress?

faqs.question: Can editors preview content before it goes live?

faqs.question: Can you migrate our existing content into Sanity?

points.title: Tiers and entitlements

points.title: Content gating and drip

points.title: Renewals, proration, and plan changes

points.title: Group and corporate seats

points.title: Dunning and churn recovery

points.body: Stripe wired in through idempotent, reconciled webhooks so entitlements, invoices, and reporting never drift apart.

title: Headless WordPress development
metaTitle: Headless WordPress with Next.js and React front ends
metaDescription: Headless WordPress done for the right reasons: a Next.js or React front end on the WP back end, tuned for Core Web Vitals without losing editor preview.
headline: headless WordPress when the front end earns it: a Next.js or React app on an editor-friendly WordPress back end.
intro: Headless WordPress keeps the WordPress admin your editors know while replacing the front end with a Next.js or React application served from the edge. Done for the right product it buys you faster pages, better Core Web Vitals, and a back end you can share with a mobile app. Done reflexively it costs you live preview and adds moving parts you did not need.

We build the front end against the WordPress REST or GraphQL (WPGraphQL) API, add incremental static regeneration and caching so content updates without full rebuilds, and restore the preview and draft workflow editors expect. We go headless when the front end genuinely benefits and stay monolithic when it does not, and we will tell you which case you are in before you commit.

points.title: Decoupled architecture
points.body: A Next.js or React front end consuming WordPress through the REST API or WPGraphQL, with the admin left intact for the content team.

points.title: Core Web Vitals and edge delivery
points.body: Static and incrementally regenerated pages served from a CDN, tuned for LCP, CLS, and INP on real mobile networks.

points.title: Preview and draft workflows
points.body: Live preview and draft rendering restored, so editors see changes before publishing despite the decoupled front end.

points.title: Incremental regeneration and caching
points.body: Content updates propagate through on-demand revalidation and cache invalidation rather than slow full rebuilds.

points.title: Shared back end for web and app
points.body: One WordPress content source feeding a website and a mobile or native client through the same API.

points.title: Honest trade-off assessment
points.body: We weigh the editor experience, preview needs, and app footprint per project and only go headless when it genuinely pays off.

faqs.question: What do we gain and lose by going headless?
faqs.answer: You gain a faster front end, better Core Web Vitals, and a back end you can share with a mobile app or multiple sites. You lose out-of-the-box live preview, some plugin front-end features, and simplicity, since a headless setup has more moving parts. We only recommend it when the front-end benefit clearly outweighs those costs.

faqs.question: Do editors still get live preview?
faqs.answer: Yes, when we build it. Preview is the main thing teams miss going headless, so we wire draft rendering and live preview into the front end so editors can see changes before publishing. It takes deliberate engineering, but the editing experience does not have to regress.

faqs.question: REST API or WPGraphQL?
faqs.answer: It depends on the front end. WPGraphQL is efficient when views need specific, nested data and helps avoid over-fetching, while the REST API is simpler and well supported for straightforward needs. We choose based on the data shape your front end actually requires rather than a fixed preference.

title: WordPress plugin development

headline: business logic belongs in a versioned plugin, not functions.php: we build WordPress plugins like software.

Nothing is hard-coded that should be configurable, plugins are versioned in git and deployed through CI rather than the admin upload screen, and each is designed with a clean upgrade path so it can be replaced one piece at a time. Whether you need a single feature or a suite of plugins behind a business platform, we write code that survives theme switches, core updates, and years of maintenance.

points.title: Plugins, not theme glue

points.title: WordPress coding standards

points.title: Configurable, never hard-coded

points.title: REST API and integrations
points.body: Custom REST endpoints and third-party integrations where the plugin needs to talk to other systems, with secure, rate-limit-aware handling.

points.title: Versioned and CI-deployed

points.title: Secure and upgrade-safe

faqs.question: Can you build a plugin to extend WooCommerce or another plugin?

faqs.question: Will the plugin survive WordPress core and theme updates?

faqs.question: Do you distribute plugins on the WordPress.org repository or keep them private?

faqs.question: Can search handle a large, cross-referenced knowledge base?

faqs.question: How do you handle moderation and editorial review?

title: Technical SEO for SaaS

intro: Most SaaS products are single-page apps: the marketing site, docs and blog render behind JavaScript, and Googlebot often receives an empty shell before the app hydrates. The content is there for users and invisible to search — so pages that should rank never get indexed, and growth that depends on being found stalls.

We do the technical side: move the routes that matter to server-side or static rendering, fix the crawl and indexing reasons pages fall out, ship structured data, and take Core Web Vitals to green. Everything is verified in Search Console and CrUX field data, not a one-off lab score.

points.title: Rendering & JavaScript SEO

points.title: Indexing & crawl budget

points.title: Core Web Vitals

points.title: Marketing site vs app split
points.body: The logged-out marketing, docs and blog kept fast and indexable without dragging the authenticated app into the same rendering path.

points.title: Structured data
points.body: Schema for software, breadcrumb, FAQ and article that earns rich results without tripping a manual action.

points.title: Migration & framework moves
points.body: App Router upgrades, replatforms and domain moves shipped with redirects mapped and rankings preserved.

faqs.question: Why aren't my JavaScript pages ranking?
faqs.answer: Usually Google receives an empty shell before your app hydrates. We confirm it in the URL Inspection rendered HTML, then move the affected routes to SSR or static rendering so the content is in the initial response.

faqs.question: Do you write the content or just the technical side?
faqs.answer: The technical side: rendering, indexing, crawlability, speed and structured data. The words stay yours; we make sure Google can actually see and rank them.

faqs.question: Can you work with our existing Next.js or React stack?

title: Cloudflare edge engineering
metaTitle: Cloudflare edge engineering: Workers, cache, WAF, R2
metaDescription: Cloudflare done properly: Workers at the edge, cache rules that actually hit, R2 and CDN offload, WAF and DNS. Lower origin load and faster global response.
headline: Cloudflare configured by engineers who read the docs, not a dashboard left on defaults.
intro: Cloudflare sits in front of a large share of the web, but most accounts use a fraction of it: the proxy is switched on and everything else is left on defaults. The value is at the edge — Workers, cache rules, R2, WAF and smart routing — and none of it configures itself.

We engineer the edge for your app specifically: cache what should be cached so most requests never reach origin, run logic in Workers close to users, offload media to R2 with no egress fees, and lock things down with WAF and rate limiting. The result is lower origin cost and faster response worldwide, with the numbers to show it.

points.title: Workers & edge logic
points.body: Redirects, A/B tests, auth checks, personalisation and API shaping run at the edge in milliseconds, off your origin.

points.title: Cache rules that hit
points.body: Cache-Control, tiered cache and cache keys tuned so HTML and assets serve from the edge instead of round-tripping to origin.

points.title: R2 & media offload
points.body: Object storage with no egress fees fronting your images and downloads, wired to the CDN and image resizing.

points.title: WAF, bot & rate limiting
points.body: Managed rules, custom firewall expressions and rate limits that stop abuse without blocking real users or Googlebot.

points.title: DNS & traffic
points.body: DNS, load balancing, failover and Argo smart routing set up for uptime and low latency across regions.

points.title: Observability
points.body: Logpush, analytics and alerting so you can see cache hit ratio, origin load and blocked traffic rather than guessing.

faqs.question: We already have Cloudflare switched on. What would change?
faqs.answer: Most accounts run on defaults: proxy enabled, everything else untouched. The gains come from cache rules, Workers and WAF configured for your app, which is where cache hit ratio and origin cost actually move.

faqs.question: Can you move us to R2 from egress-heavy storage?
faqs.answer: Yes. R2 has no egress fees, so media-heavy sites usually see a real drop in the bill. We migrate the objects, front them with the CDN and update your references.

faqs.question: Do you work with the free plan or only Enterprise?
faqs.answer: Both. Much of what matters — cache rules, Workers, WAF basics, R2 — is available well below Enterprise. We build for the plan you're on and only recommend an upgrade when the numbers justify it.

title: Programmatic SEO engineering
metaTitle: Programmatic SEO engineering: template pages at scale
metaDescription: Template-driven SEO pages built to index and last: clean data, unique-enough content, fast rendering and a sitemap architecture Google can actually crawl.
headline: template-scale SEO pages engineered to index and last, not a thin-content penalty waiting to happen.
intro: Programmatic SEO turns a dataset into thousands of pages aimed at long-tail intent. Done badly, it produces near-duplicate, thin pages that Google either ignores or actively penalises. Done well, it is a durable channel that keeps compounding.

We treat it as an engineering problem: the data model, the templating, internal linking, crawl budget and rendering. The pages come out distinct enough to index, fast enough to rank, and maintainable as the underlying data changes — and we only publish the ones that clear the bar.

points.title: Data model & sources
points.body: A clean, deduplicated dataset behind the pages, because the content quality is capped by the quality of the data.

points.title: Templates that don't read as templates
points.body: Enough unique, genuinely useful content per page that Google indexes it rather than folding it into a duplicate cluster.

points.title: Rendering & speed
points.body: Static generation or SSR so tens of thousands of pages ship as real HTML and pass Core Web Vitals.

points.title: Internal linking & architecture
points.body: Hub-and-spoke linking, breadcrumbs and a sitemap structure that spend crawl budget where it counts.

points.title: Indexing control
points.body: Canonicalisation, noindex on thin variants and coverage monitoring so you scale without diluting the index.

points.title: Iteration & measurement
points.body: Coverage, impressions and rankings tracked per template, so you double down on what indexes and cut what doesn't.

faqs.question: Isn't programmatic SEO just thin content Google penalises?
faqs.answer: It is when the pages are near-duplicates with no added value. The engineering is in making each page genuinely useful and distinct from the same data, and in publishing only the pages that clear that bar.

faqs.question: How many pages can you generate?
faqs.answer: As many as the data supports — hundreds to hundreds of thousands. The limit is useful, unique data, not the build. We'd rather ship 5,000 pages that index than 50,000 that don't.

faqs.question: Will these pages slow the site down?
faqs.answer: No. We render them statically or server-side so they serve as fast HTML, and we keep them out of the request path of your core app.

title: WordPress performance optimisation
metaTitle: WordPress performance optimisation: Core Web Vitals
metaDescription: Make WordPress fast: Core Web Vitals to green, caching and CDN done right, database and plugin bloat cut, and TTFB fixed at the source. Measured in field data.
headline: WordPress taken to green on Core Web Vitals, fixed at the source instead of buried under another cache plugin.
intro: Most WordPress sites are slow for the same handful of reasons: too many plugins, an unoptimised database, render-blocking CSS and JavaScript, a bloated theme, and a host doing too much work on every request. Stacking another cache plugin hides the problem; it doesn't fix it.

We profile where the time actually goes — TTFB, queries, assets, third-party scripts — and fix the causes. Server-level caching, a properly configured CDN, modern image and font handling, database cleanup, and cutting the plugins that cost more than they're worth. Progress is measured in CrUX field data, not a single Lighthouse number.

points.title: Diagnose the real bottleneck
points.body: Profiling with Query Monitor, server timing and field data to find where the milliseconds are lost, before touching anything.

points.title: TTFB & caching
points.body: Full-page and object caching at the server level with Redis, page cache and OPcache, so most requests never hit PHP or the database.

points.title: CDN & media
points.body: A properly configured CDN, modern formats like WebP and AVIF, lazy-loading and offloaded media so assets load fast worldwide.

points.title: Database & plugins
points.body: Bloated tables, autoloaded options and old revisions cleaned up, and heavy plugins replaced or removed rather than tolerated.

points.title: Front-end & Core Web Vitals
points.body: Render-blocking CSS and JavaScript, layout shift and slow LCP fixed in the theme so the vitals pass in CrUX field data.

points.title: Hosting & stack
points.body: Honest advice on when the host or PHP version is the ceiling, and a move to something that isn't.

faqs.question: Won't a caching plugin do this?
faqs.answer: Caching helps once the underlying site is sound, but it hides slow queries and bloated pages rather than fixing them. We fix the causes first, then cache — otherwise you're just caching a slow page.

faqs.question: Do I need to go headless to be fast?
faqs.answer: Usually not. Most WordPress sites can pass Core Web Vitals on a well-configured LiteSpeed or LEMP stack. Headless is worth it when the front-end genuinely warrants it, not as a prerequisite for speed.

faqs.question: How do you prove the site got faster?
faqs.answer: Field-data Core Web Vitals from CrUX and Search Console, plus lab profiling and TTFB and LCP numbers, before and after. We report the measurements, not a single score.
